lessons.title: Thermodynamic Cycles
lessons.objective: Apply the Otto and Diesel cycles to aero piston engine operation: relate the four strokes to crankshaft and piston movement, read the ideal and practical Otto pressure-volume diagram, explain valve lead, lag and overlap, and distinguish the Diesel cycle by how it adds heat and starts combustion - while keeping ideal teaching diagrams separate from manufacturer timing and measured pressure data.
lessons.purpose: Explain the scientific principle by which thermal energy can eventually produce mechanical work.
outcomes: Explain the concept of a heat engine.
Explain why thermodynamic cycles are used as simplified models of real engine processes.
Identify basic thermodynamic processes involving pressure, volume, heat addition and heat rejection.
Explain the constant-volume process.
Interpret a simple pressure-volume diagram.
Describe the ideal Carnot cycle as a conceptual reference for heat-engine efficiency.
Describe and illustrate the ideal Otto cycle using a P–V diagram.
Distinguish the theoretical Otto cycle from the practical piston-engine cycle.
Describe and illustrate the Diesel cycle.
Differentiate the Diesel cycle from the Otto cycle.
Explain the basic combustion process of a Diesel engine.
Explain major limitations of Diesel engines in aircraft applications.
Recognise the Brayton cycle as the thermodynamic basis of gas-turbine engines.
Distinguish a thermodynamic cycle from a mechanical operating cycle.
Compare two-stroke and four-stroke operation.
Relate crankshaft rotation to piston movement over an operating cycle.
Recognise that practical valve events do not occur exactly at TDC and BDC.
lessons.syllabusNote: These are directly aligned with the formal Otto and Diesel outcomes in the module description.
lessons.completionCriteria: Explain a heat engine and why a cycle is used as a model of one; name the basic processes (constant volume, constant pressure, constant temperature, no heat exchange); read a pressure-volume diagram and say what its loop encloses; describe the Carnot cycle as the efficiency limit; describe the ideal Otto cycle, tell it from the practical one, and say why combustion is treated as constant volume; describe the Diesel cycle, tell it from the Otto cycle, and say what limits diesels in aircraft; recognise the Brayton cycle as the gas turbine's; tell a thermodynamic cycle from a mechanical operating cycle, compare two-stroke and four-stroke operation, relate crankshaft rotation to piston movement, and explain why valve events do not fall exactly at TDC and BDC - without treating an illustrative diagram as measured engine data.

steps.title: What cycle means
steps.prompt:
An operating cycle describes how an engine repeats the events needed to turn fuel energy into shaft rotation.

Before looking at the four named cycles, predict which features belong to the cycle itself and which belong to another classification, such as cylinder layout or cooling method.
steps.note: Documented classification frame from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46-48, cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 20-23. This step frames the lesson using the instructor's learning outcomes; it is not an assessed fact.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short prediction establishes the classification boundary more clearly than a visual.

steps.title: Heat engines
steps.prompt:
An engine takes the energy stored in fuel and turns it into work. The FAA handbook calls a machine that does this through heat a heat engine: it converts the chemical energy in a fuel into heat energy, and that heat is then converted into mechanical energy and useful work.

Every heat engine follows one pattern. It takes in heat from something hot, converts part of it to work, and must discard the rest as heat to something cooler. In a piston engine the hot source is the burning charge, and the cooler place is the surrounding air that takes the exhaust and the cooling air.

Thermal efficiency is the work out divided by the heat in. Because some heat is always rejected, the exhaust is hot and the engine needs cooling.
steps.note: Heat engine as defined in the FAA handbook glossary (FAA-H-8083-32B, PDF p. 472); hot source, work and discarded heat, and thermal efficiency W / Qh = 1 - Qc / Qh from OpenStax University Physics Volume 2, 4.2, checked 13 October 2026.

mediaPlan.rationale: A simple flow diagram of heat in, work out and heat rejected makes the pattern visible at a glance.
mediaPlan.assetBrief: A labelled energy-flow diagram: heat from burning fuel goes in, shaft work comes out, and the remaining heat leaves with the exhaust and the cooling air. No invented percentages.

steps.title: Four-stroke sequence
steps.prompt: Use the crank-angle scrubber to move through intake, compression, power and exhaust. Watch one complete cycle require two crankshaft revolutions while the piston completes four strokes.
steps.note: Documented sequence from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46-48. The planned animation will show phase, piston direction and ideal valve state only; it will not display invented pressure, temperature or flow values.

mediaPlan.rationale: Scrubbing a 720-degree state makes the repeated sequence and two-revolution relationship observable.

steps.title: Intake pose
steps.prompt: At 90 degrees, predict the piston's direction and which ideal-cycle valve should be open. Reveal the GTSIO-520-H teaching-cylinder pose, then separate what the model proves geometrically from what its coloured gas cue only illustrates.
steps.note: Documented four-stroke sequence from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46-48. The mechanism pose is profile-checked; valve and gas cues remain an ideal teaching profile, not certified GTSIO-520-H timing or CFD.

mediaPlan.rationale: The existing operating-cylinder model directly shows the crank, rod and piston relationship at a chosen angle.

steps.title: Power pose
steps.prompt: At 450 degrees the piston is travelling the same direction as at 90 degrees, yet compression has come and gone in between. Compare the two poses: which mechanical motion repeats, and which cycle event has changed?
steps.note: Documented four-stroke sequence from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46-48. In the shared 720-degree teaching profile 0-180 is intake, 180-360 compression, 360-540 power and 540-720 exhaust, so 450 degrees is mid-power stroke; the profile distinguishes the second crankshaft revolution from the first.

mediaPlan.rationale: A paired pose comparison (both poses descending) shows why piston direction alone does not identify the stroke.

steps.title: Strokes and events
steps.prompt:
Two different things are called a cycle, and it helps to keep them apart.

The mechanical cycle is about the hardware. In a four-stroke engine the piston makes four strokes of 180 degrees of crankshaft turn each, so one cycle takes 720 degrees: two turns of the crankshaft, with one power stroke per cylinder.

The thermodynamic cycle is about the gas: the series of states it passes through, its pressure, volume and temperature at each, and where heat is added and removed.

They line up, but not exactly. The handbook names five events: intake, compression, ignition, power and exhaust. Strokes are the piston's motion; events are what happens to the charge, and they overlap the strokes. The spark fires before TDC, still in the compression stroke, and the exhaust valve opens before the piston reaches BDC.
steps.note: Four strokes, two crankshaft revolutions (720 degrees) and the five events (intake, compression, ignition, power, exhaust) from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 46; ignition before TDC and the early exhaust-valve opening from PDF p. 48; the strokes-versus-events distinction also appears on course slide 54. The handbook says the four-stroke cycle is 'sometimes called the Otto cycle'; in this lesson the Otto cycle names the ideal model of the gas, not the stroke count.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Why use a model?
steps.prompt:
A real cylinder is a messy place. The gas is a mixture of air, fuel vapour and leftover exhaust. Burning takes time. Heat leaks into the walls, some gas slips past the rings, and the valves open and close over many degrees of crankshaft turn. No simple equation follows all of that at once.

So engineers use a simplified model. In the ideal cycles a fixed mass of air stands in for the working gas and behaves as an ideal gas. The burning and exhausting are replaced by heat added and heat removed in a few clean processes.

A model is not a measurement. Its value is that it is simple enough to reason with: it shows what raises or lowers the work, and where the limit lies. Later steps show how far a real engine departs from it.
steps.note: The ideal cycle as a model on a fixed mass of air with ideal-gas relations, and the remark that the actual cycle lacks its sharp transitions: MIT Unified Engineering, Thermodynamics and Propulsion, section 3.5. Assumptions of the ideal cycle (no heat exchange in compression and power, no friction, instantaneous combustion) and the real-engine losses: NASA Glenn Otto cycle page and course slides 56 and 57. Valve opening over several degrees and residual exhaust: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 47 to 48. Checked 13 October 2026.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Four basic processes
steps.prompt:
Every cycle is built from a few simple processes. Each holds one thing steady while the others change.

Constant volume (isochoric): the piston does not move, so no work is done. Heat added raises the pressure and temperature.

Constant pressure (isobaric): the volume changes while the pressure stays the same.

Constant temperature (isothermal): heat flows in or out so that the temperature does not change.

No heat exchange (adiabatic): the gas is neither heated nor cooled, so compressing it raises its temperature and expanding it lowers it.

In any of them heat can be added or rejected, and work can be done on the gas or by it. A cycle is a chain of such processes that ends where it began.
steps.note: Definitions of isobaric, isochoric, isothermal and adiabatic processes from OpenStax University Physics Volume 2, 3.4; no work at constant volume from OpenStax College Physics 2e, 15.2; the course slides call the reversible adiabatic compression and expansion isentropic. Checked 13 October 2026.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Reading a pressure-volume diagram
steps.prompt:
A pressure-volume (PV) diagram plots the gas's pressure against its volume. Each point is a state of the gas, and the path joining the points shows a process.

Read it like a map. Moving right, the volume grows and the gas is expanding; moving left, it is being compressed. Moving up, the pressure rises. A vertical line is a constant-volume process and a horizontal line is a constant-pressure one.

The area under a path is the work done. Over a full cycle the loop encloses the net work: what the gas gives on expansion, minus what it takes to compress it. A loop traced clockwise gives net work out, which is what an engine needs.

A bigger loop means more work from every cycle.
steps.note: Work as the area under a path, no work at constant volume, and the enclosed loop (positive when clockwise) from OpenStax College Physics 2e, 15.2; the enclosed area as net indicated work per cycle also appears on course slide 58 and on the NASA Glenn Otto cycle page. Checked 13 October 2026.

mediaPlan.rationale: A labelled pair of axes shows how to read direction, steady lines and the enclosed area before the engine diagrams appear.
mediaPlan.assetBrief: A schematic, unscaled PV diagram: volume on the horizontal axis, pressure on the vertical, a clockwise loop shaded, arrows showing the direction of travel and a note saying that the area inside is the net work. No engine data.

steps.title: The Carnot limit
steps.prompt:
In 1824 Sadi Carnot proposed an ideal cycle with the highest efficiency any engine can have between two temperatures. Its four processes are: heat taken in at constant temperature, an expansion with no heat exchange, heat given out at constant temperature, and a compression with no heat exchange.

Its efficiency depends only on the two temperatures, in kelvin:

efficiency = 1 - (cold temperature / hot temperature)

With a hot source at 1,000 K and a cold sink at 300 K, that is 1 - 0.3 = 70 percent.

The hotter the source or the colder the sink, the higher the limit. Only a sink at 0 K would give 100 percent, so every heat engine must reject some heat. Real engines fall below their limit: the handbook puts a reciprocating aircraft engine at about 34 percent thermal efficiency, the rest leaving through the exhaust, the cooling and friction.
steps.note: The Carnot cycle (proposed 1824), its four processes, e = 1 - Tc / Th and the statement that real engines between the same reservoirs are less efficient: OpenStax University Physics Volume 2, 4.5, checked 13 October 2026. Reciprocating engines about 34 percent thermally efficient: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 56. The 1,000 K and 300 K figures are an illustration, not engine data.

mediaPlan.rationale: A small calculator showing how the limit moves as the two temperatures change gives the formula meaning.
mediaPlan.assetBrief: A native-HTML slider pair for hot and cold temperature in kelvin that shows the Carnot efficiency, labelled as an illustration of the formula only.

steps.title: Ideal Otto cycle
steps.prompt: A pressure-volume (PV) diagram plots the cylinder's pressure against its volume through one cycle. Step through the ideal Otto cycle and watch the piston beside it. Which two processes hold the volume constant, and which two have no heat exchange?
steps.note: Neither FAA-H-8083-32B nor EASA Module 16 covers pressure-volume diagram theory (both searched 29 September 2026). Ideal Otto processes (two adiabatic, two constant-volume) are from the instructor's course deck, slides 56 and 58 (tier 4), and the Wikipedia Otto cycle article (tier 5, CC BY-SA 4.0, accessed 29 September 2026). The curves are schematic ideal-gas shapes, not data for any engine. Cross-checked against MIT Unified Engineering, 'Thermodynamics and Propulsion' section 3.5 (isentropic compression and expansion; constant-volume combustion and heat rejection; tier 4 textbook-grade source) and NASA Glenn's Otto cycle page (combustion at constant volume; no heat exchange during the compression and power strokes).

mediaPlan.rationale: Stepping a marker around the loop while the piston moves shows how each process links to a stroke.

steps.title: Why constant volume?
steps.prompt:
The ideal cycle treats combustion as instant heat addition while the piston sits at top dead centre. The volume cannot change, so no work is done during that process: all the heat goes into the gas, and its pressure and temperature jump straight up.

That is what constant volume means here.

Real burning takes time, which is why the spark fires before TDC (20 to 35 degrees before, on the engines the handbook describes) and cylinder pressure peaks a little after it. The ideal loop also leaves out the pumping done on the intake and exhaust strokes.
steps.note: No work at constant volume: OpenStax College Physics 2e, 15.2, and MIT Unified Engineering section 3.5 (heat input equals the change in internal energy during combustion). Ignition timing of 20 to 35 degrees before TDC: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48. The ideal Otto assumptions are from course slide 56 and the NASA Glenn Otto cycle page. Checked 13 October 2026.

mediaPlan.rationale: The constant-volume idea is stated once, directly after the diagram that shows it.

steps.title: Ideal versus practical
steps.prompt: Switch between the ideal and practical diagrams. Find two differences in shape, then link each to a physical cause: burning takes time, heat is lost to the cylinder walls, and valves open early and close late.
steps.note: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 48 and 51 (Figure 1-39) documents the actual cylinder-pressure diagram and its peak after top center. The list of causes follows the course deck, slides 57-58 (tier 4). The practical curve is an illustrative rounding of the ideal loop, not measured data. MIT section 3.5 notes the actual cycle lacks the sharp transitions between processes that the ideal cycle has, and NASA Glenn notes the real cycle's enclosed area (work) is always less than the ideal value.

mediaPlan.rationale: Overlaying the ideal loop as a dashed line makes each departure from the ideal visible.

steps.title: Valve lead, lag and overlap
steps.prompt: Move the crank through the FAA example timing chart. Find where each valve opens and closes relative to TDC and BDC, and locate the interval around TDC when both valves are open.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 47, Figure 1-37 (example valve timing chart) and its text: valve events vary considerably in different engines, and the manufacturer's recommendations must be followed. The chart values are an FAA example, not GTSIO-520-H timing; the GTSIO-520 manual searched here gives no valve timing figures. The instructor accepted the FAA example chart for this lesson (29 September 2026).

mediaPlan.rationale: A crank-angle marker over a two-revolution timeline shows valve state and overlap at any angle.

steps.title: Why overlap helps
steps.prompt:
The intake valve opens before TDC on the exhaust stroke (valve lead), and the exhaust valve closes after TDC (valve lag).

The overlap cools the cylinder internally with cool incoming charge, draws in more mixture and helps scavenge burnt gas. It works because moving gas has momentum: the outgoing exhaust leaves the cylinder at low pressure, which speeds the fresh charge in.

Timing is limited, though. Open the intake too early and hot gas can flash back; close it too late and charge can be pushed back out.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 47-48 (valve lead, valve lag, valve overlap, scavenging effect and the limits on early opening and late closing).

mediaPlan.rationale: The merits and limits of lead and lag follow the diagram that defines them.

steps.title: Two-stroke and four-stroke
steps.prompt:
Most certified aircraft engines are four-stroke. Each cylinder needs two turns of the crankshaft for one power stroke, and valves control the gas.

A two-stroke engine completes the operating cycle in one turn: one upstroke and one downstroke. Intake and exhaust happen during the same stroke, and every revolution brings a power stroke. The handbook notes that two-strokes are used in ultra-light, light sport and experimental aircraft, and generally need a gear reduction between engine and propeller.

The course slides weigh them like this. The four-stroke burns cleanly and economically and lasts longer between overhauls, but is heavier with more parts. The two-stroke is light and simple, but uses more fuel and wears sooner.

A rotary engine has no reciprocating piston at all: a three-sided rotor turns inside an elliptical housing. Follow either link for the detail; neither is needed to continue.
steps.note: Four-stroke cycle (two revolutions) and two-stroke cycle (one revolution, intake and exhaust in the same stroke, gear reduction, ultra-light and light sport use) from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46 and 48; rotary rotor and housing from PDF p. 48; EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 19-23. The comparison of strengths and weaknesses is the instructor's course slides (the four-stroke and two-stroke slides): they are generalisations, not measured data. The two-stroke and rotary cycles are standalone deep-dive lessons.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this comparison; the deep-dive lessons hold the diagrams.

steps.title: Diesel versus Otto
steps.prompt: Compare the two ideal cycles. Both start with the same compression, so predict which one process differs before you toggle, and what that means for how the fuel burns. Then raise the compression ratio and notice how each loop changes.
steps.note: Diesel cycle description documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48, and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 23; EASA PDF p. 210 notes the diesel compression ratio is far greater than a gasoline engine's. The constant-pressure heat-addition process is from the course deck, slide 76 (tier 4), and Wikipedia Diesel cycle (tier 5, CC BY-SA 4.0, accessed 29 September 2026). Neither FAA-H-8083-32B nor EASA Module 16 covers pressure-volume diagram theory (both searched 29 September 2026). Curves are schematic. Cross-checked against MIT section 3.6: compression ignition, fuel sprayed in once compression is complete, and a higher compression ratio is possible because only air is compressed with no risk of auto-ignition.

mediaPlan.rationale: Overlaying the two loops isolates the single process that differs: constant-volume versus constant-pressure heat addition.

steps.title: Diesel combustion
steps.prompt:
A diesel-cycle engine first compresses air alone. Near maximum pressure, fuel is sprayed in, and the high pressure and temperature make it burn without a spark. The rising pressure drives the piston down.

Because the fuel burns as it is injected, the ideal diesel cycle adds heat at roughly constant pressure while the piston moves away from TDC.

'Diesel' names the ignition strategy. Two-stroke and four-stroke diesels both exist.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48, and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 23. Constant-pressure heat addition from the course deck, slide 76 (tier 4). Replaces the earlier single 'Diesel ignition' step; the spark-versus-compression comparison now lives in lesson 5. Cross-checked against MIT section 3.6 (fuel sprayed into the cylinder when compression is complete; ignition without a spark).

mediaPlan.rationale: The combustion sequence is short and follows the diagram just studied.

steps.title: Diesel in aviation
steps.prompt:
Diesel-cycle engines can burn Jet A, but regulators raised specific concerns when they returned to small aeroplanes.

Turbine fuel must be accommodated in fuel systems designed for gasoline. A conventional diesel vibrates badly if one cylinder stops firing, which can damage the airframe and propeller. High internal pressures mean cylinder parts could be shed in a failure. The engine needs FADEC control with its own limits and indications.

Add heavier construction, complex fuel injection, long cold-weather cranking and the risk of misfuelling.
steps.note: Aero-specific concerns are from the FAA's proposed special conditions for the Piper PA-28-236 with an SMA SR305-230 diesel engine (Federal Register vol. 71 no. 114, 14 June 2006): turbine fuel in gasoline-designed systems, vibration and failure modes with a cylinder inoperative, high-energy fragments from high internal pressures, FADEC control, and limitations and indications. The FAA states these concerns are not universally applicable to all diesel engines. Heavier construction, complex injection and cold cranking are from the course deck, slide 78 (tier 4); misfuelling from EASA Module 16, PDF p. 228. The FAA and EASA handbook texts contain no limitations list, so per the instructor's decision (29 September 2026) this step uses the FAA notice, the deck and common engineering sense.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short list of concerns needs no visual.

steps.title: The Brayton cycle
steps.prompt:
Gas turbines run on a different cycle, the Brayton cycle. The handbook describes four events that are continuous rather than taking turns: intake, compression, expansion and exhaust, each going on all the time in a different part of the engine.

Air is drawn in and compressed. Fuel burns in the combustion chamber, heating the air so that it expands while the pressure stays about constant, which is why the handbook calls it the constant-pressure cycle, or the continuous combustion cycle. The hot gas then drives the turbine and leaves through the exhaust.

Compare the piston engine, where the same cylinder takes each event in turn. The Otto and Diesel cycles repeat in a cylinder; the Brayton cycle runs as a flow. Lesson 2 met the turbine engine; this is its cycle.
steps.note: The Brayton cycle as the thermodynamic cycle of the gas turbine, a variable-volume constant-pressure cycle also called the continuous combustion cycle with four continuous events (intake, compression, expansion, exhaust): FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 79. Compression, combustion at constant pressure, turbine and nozzle expansion, and its use in all gas turbine engines: NASA Glenn Beginner's Guide, Brayton cycle. Checked 13 October 2026.

mediaPlan.rationale: A schematic gas turbine with the four events labelled along its length shows why the cycle is a flow.
mediaPlan.assetBrief: A labelled outline of a turbojet or turboprop in section, with intake, compressor, combustion chamber, turbine and exhaust named, and an arrow for airflow. Schematic only; no engine data.

steps.title: Choose the evidence
steps.prompt: A diagram can establish event order and mechanical relationships. It cannot, by appearance alone, establish a real engine's valve timing, cylinder pressure, gas temperature or efficiency. Those claims need an applicable manual or a validated analytical model.
steps.note: Documented evidence boundary carried forward from the platform architecture. Manufacturer-specific timing remains controlled by the applicable engine data; FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48, explicitly directs ignition timing to the engine manufacturer's recommendation.

mediaPlan.rationale: This is an evidence-literacy synthesis step.

lessons.title: Classification
lessons.objective: Classify a piston engine on separate axes - cylinder arrangement (inline, V-type, radial, horizontally opposed) and ignition method (spark or compression) - explain how arrangement influences frontal area, cooling access, crankshaft/rod layout and installation without turning typical traits into universal rules, and read cylinder numbering and firing order from the engine manual.
lessons.purpose: Show students that the same engine can be classified in several different ways depending on the characteristic being considered.
outcomes: Explain the purpose of classifying aircraft piston engines.
Classify engines according to cylinder arrangement.
Recognise inline, V-type, horizontally opposed, radial and historically relevant rotary arrangements.
Classify engines according to the number of cylinders.
Explain why individual engine cylinders must be numbered.
Describe common cylinder-numbering conventions and relate numbering to maintenance, firing order and fault identification.
Classify engines as air-cooled or liquid-cooled.
Classify engines as two-stroke or four-stroke.
Distinguish spark-ignition and compression-ignition engines.
Distinguish naturally aspirated, supercharged and turbocharged engines.
Distinguish carburetted and fuel-injected engines.
Distinguish direct-drive and geared engines.
Compare broad advantages and disadvantages of the major engine arrangements.
lessons.syllabusNote: Cylinder arrangement, general classification and cylinder numbering are explicitly required in the source curriculum.
lessons.completionCriteria: Say why engines are classified and place an engine on each axis: cylinder arrangement (inline, V-type, radial, horizontally opposed, and the historical rotary), number of cylinders, cooling (air or liquid), cycle (two-stroke or four-stroke), ignition (spark or compression), aspiration (naturally aspirated, supercharged or turbocharged), fuelling (carburetted or fuel-injected) and propeller drive (direct or geared); give the typical strengths and limits of each arrangement without treating them as universal; explain why cylinders are numbered, read the numbering and firing order from the manual, and read a model name such as GTSIO-520-H as a classification.

steps.title: One engine, many labels
steps.prompt:
The manufacturer's overhaul manual describes the GTSIO-520 as a six-cylinder, horizontally opposed, geared, turbocharged, fuel-injected, air-cooled, four-cycle engine. One sentence, seven labels.

Classifying means sorting engines by one characteristic at a time: how the cylinders are arranged, how many there are, how they are cooled, how the propeller is driven. The handbook sorts reciprocating engines by operating cycle, by cylinder arrangement and by cooling, and more axes follow from that.

Why bother? A label tells you what to expect: what the engine looks like, how it is cooled, what maintenance it needs. The same engine sits in a different group on every axis.

Before reading on, which of the seven labels describes the arrangement of the cylinders?
steps.note: The manual's description of the basic GTSIO-520 (overhaul manual X30045A, section I, paragraph 1-2) and the handbook's classification by operating cycle, cylinder arrangement and cooling (FAA-H-8083-32B, PDF p. 24). This step frames the lesson using the instructor's learning outcomes; it is not an assessed fact.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short prediction prompt sets up the lesson; the labels themselves are the content.

steps.title: Inline bank
steps.prompt: Identify the single straight bank and the crankshaft above or below it. Compare upright and inverted installations, and notice the small frontal area of the arrangement.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 24. Use an FAA source figure or an accuracy-checked redraw; retain the upright/inverted distinction.

mediaPlan.rationale: An accuracy-checked schematic communicates the single-bank geometry without implying a specific engine.

steps.title: V-type banks
steps.prompt: Find the two inline banks sharing one crankshaft. Use the bank angle and common crankshaft to distinguish a V engine from two separate inline engines.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 25. The handbook describes two inline banks, generally set 60 degrees apart; the lesson should avoid implying that every V engine uses the same angle or cylinder count.

mediaPlan.rationale: The defining relationship is geometric and reads best in a controlled front-view schematic.

steps.title: Radial rows
steps.prompt: Trace one row of cylinders around the central crankcase. Then compare a single row with multiple staggered rows and identify why the front view, not a side silhouette alone, is needed to recognise the arrangement.
steps.alt: FAA single-row and double-row radial engine examples
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 25-27. Use FAA Figures 1-2 and 1-3 as the first-choice visual source.

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook figures already show the single-row and double-row geometry accurately.

steps.title: Rotary: the engine that spins
steps.prompt:
In this course "rotary" means two different things.

The rotary radial engine, used in some early aircraft, turns the usual arrangement inside out. The crankshaft is rigidly attached to the airframe, and the propeller, crankcase and cylinders all revolve as a unit around it. The seven-cylinder Gnome rotaries of the First World War are the classic example. The spinning cylinders were cooled by the air rushing over them.

The other rotary is the rotary-combustion engine: a three-sided rotor turning inside an elliptical housing, with no cylinders at all. That is a different operating cycle, met in lesson 4's deep dive, not a cylinder arrangement.

The revolving-cylinder rotary is history, but the outcomes ask you to recognise it.
steps.note: Rotary radial engine as defined in the FAA handbook glossary (FAA-H-8083-32B, glossary entry in PDF pp. 455 to 490); the Gnome Omega as a seven-cylinder, air-cooled rotary of 50 hp at 1,200 rpm from the Smithsonian record; cooling by the spinning cylinders passing through the air from course slides 19 to 21 (instructor deck, not independently verified). The three-sided rotor and elliptical housing are from the handbook, PDF p. 48.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Opposed engine
steps.prompt: Orbit the six-cylinder GTSIO-520-H and identify the two banks directly opposite one another with the crankshaft between them. Predict which view makes the opposed layout most obvious before revealing the model.
steps.note: Documented general arrangement from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 24-25. The GTSIO-520 overhaul manual identifies the basic engine as six-cylinder, horizontally opposed (PDF p. 13). The current whole-engine mesh is a teaching reconstruction and must retain its modelling-status disclosure.

mediaPlan.rationale: Free orbit makes the two opposed banks and central crankshaft spatially obvious.

steps.title: Arrangement compare
steps.prompt: Switch among inline, V-type, radial and opposed outlines. Rotate the same notional engine axis and compare bank count, cylinder direction and frontal outline without changing the operating cycle.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 24-25, and EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 23-25. The comparator will use schematic silhouettes, not claim exact dimensions for a real engine.

mediaPlan.rationale: A single controlled comparator prevents scale and viewpoint changes from obscuring the geometry difference.

steps.title: What each arrangement offers
steps.prompt:
Each arrangement is a trade-off. These are the typical traits the FAA handbook gives.

Inline: a small frontal area and good streamlining. Mounted inverted, it also allows a shorter landing gear and better pilot visibility. But air-cooled inlines get harder to cool as they grow, so they stayed small and low-powered.

V-type: two inline banks, generally 60 degrees apart, mostly with twelve cylinders, liquid or air cooled. Chiefly a Second World War engine.

Radial: very rugged and dependable. Still found in some older cargo aircraft, war birds and crop sprayers.

Opposed: a low weight for its power, a narrow silhouette that suits wing installation, and low vibration. The air-cooled version is the one used predominantly in aviation.
steps.note: Typical advantages and uses of the inline, opposed, V-type and radial arrangements from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 24 to 25. The handbook states these as general tendencies, not rules for every engine of a type.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Configuration, not verdict
steps.prompt: Arrangement affects packaging, cooling paths, balance and maintenance access, but it does not decide the whole engine. Cooling, ignition, aspiration, materials and installation still matter. Treat each stated advantage or limitation as typical and source-bounded, not universal.
steps.note: Documented synthesis of the FAA and EASA configuration sections. This boundary prevents the lesson from turning a layout label into an unsupported claim about every engine of that type.

mediaPlan.rationale: The closing distinction is conceptual.

steps.title: How many cylinders?
steps.prompt:
Engines can also be sorted by how many cylinders they have, and the count follows from the layout.

An inline engine generally has an even number, although some three-cylinder engines have been built. Opposed engines pair their cylinders across the crankshaft: the handbook shows a four-cylinder opposed engine, and the GTSIO-520-H has six. V-types mostly have twelve.

Radial engines are counted in rows. A row may have three, five, seven or nine cylinders. Double-row radials stack two rows of seven or nine, and one type has four rows of seven, 28 cylinders in all.

The count alone does not give the size of the engine. Displacement is the swept volume of one cylinder times the number of cylinders.
steps.note: Cylinder counts for each arrangement from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 24 to 25. Displacement as swept volume times the number of cylinders: the course slide with the worked displacement example for a Continental 520 cylinder, and the manual figures for the GTSIO-520 (bore 5.25 in, stroke 4.00 in, 520 cubic inches).

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Why number the cylinders?
steps.prompt:
The cylinders of a six-cylinder engine look nearly identical, yet a technician has to say which one has the low compression, the fouled plug or the high head temperature.

Numbering gives every cylinder a name that all the manuals, logbooks and gauge readings can share. It also gives the engine a fixed starting point. The overhaul manual times the magnetos from the No. 1 cylinder, and the propeller keyway is indexed to No. 1 cylinder top dead centre.

Numbering needs fixed directions too. The propeller end is always the front and the accessory end the rear, and left and right are always seen from the rear, however the engine sits in the aircraft.
steps.note: Engine directions and the reason for numbering from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 36; propeller keyway indexed to No. 1 cylinder TDC, PDF p. 44; magneto installation from the No. 1 cylinder firing position, GTSIO-520 overhaul manual.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Numbering the cylinders
steps.prompt: Find cylinder No. 1, then predict where No. 2 goes. On the GTSIO-520-H the cylinders are numbered from the rear, with odd numbers on the right bank and even numbers on the left, as seen from the accessory end. Numbering is not standardised - some manufacturers number from the front - so always check the engine manual.
steps.note: Documented from the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, paragraph 1-7 and the definition of terms (PDF pp. 13-14: cylinders numbered from the rear, odd on the right and even on the left, right and left taken facing the accessory end) and FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 36-37 (left and right taken from the rear; inline and V engines numbered from the rear; opposed-engine numbering 'is by no means standard'; Figure 1-19). The IO-520 manual gives the same rule (paragraph 1-5). The whole-engine model contract (web/engine-contract.json) labels cylinder-1 as left-forward, a reconstruction that does not match the manual; the manual is followed here.

mediaPlan.rationale: A top-view diagram with the numbers on the cylinders shows the rule at a glance.

steps.title: Firing order
steps.prompt: The firing order is the sequence in which the cylinders' power events occur, chosen for balance and low vibration. Scrub the crank angle and watch the GTSIO-520-H fire 1-4-5-2-3-6, one cylinder every 120 degrees. The IO-520 has the same layout but fires 1-6-3-2-5-4, so never assume one engine's order from another's.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 37 (firing order chosen for balance; opposed engines list in pairs; a six-cylinder opposed example 1-4-5-2-3-6), the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual (PDF p. 15, and PDF p. 153 for the -H: 1-4-5-2-3-6) and the IO-520 overhaul manual Table II (1-6-3-2-5-4). The 120-degree spacing is derived (720 / 6) for teaching; the manuals give the order, not crank-angle timing.

mediaPlan.rationale: Scrubbing the crank angle shows the order as a sequence in time on the layout.

steps.title: Air or liquid cooled
steps.prompt:
Every piston engine in the end passes its excess heat to the surrounding air. What differs is how the heat gets there.

In an air-cooled engine the heat passes straight from the cylinders to the air, so the cylinders carry thin metal fins to give the air more surface to touch. Most reciprocating aircraft engines are air cooled, the GTSIO-520-H among them.

In a liquid-cooled engine the heat goes first into a coolant, which is piped to a radiator in the airstream. The main problem is the added weight of coolant, radiator and tubing. In return, liquid cooling allows high power to be obtained safely, which is why a few high-power engines use it.

Lesson 6 takes cooling apart in detail.
steps.note: Air and liquid cooling from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 24, and the glossary entries for air cooling and liquid cooling. The GTSIO-520 is described as air cooled in the manufacturer's overhaul manual.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Two-stroke or four-stroke
steps.prompt:
Lesson 4 compared the two cycles. For classification all you need is the count.

A four-stroke engine takes four strokes, two turns of the crankshaft, to finish its cycle in a cylinder. A two-stroke needs two strokes, one turn. The manual's phrase "4 cycle" means four-stroke: the GTSIO-520-H is a four-stroke, like the vast majority of certified aircraft engines. Two-strokes appear in ultra-light, light sport and experimental aircraft.

Take care with the word cycle. A manual's "4 cycle" counts strokes. The handbook also says the four-stroke cycle is sometimes called the Otto cycle, a loose use of a name that, in lesson 4, belonged to the ideal model of the gas.
steps.note: Four-stroke and two-stroke cycles, their use and the loose naming of the Otto cycle from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46 and 48; the GTSIO-520 described as a four-cycle engine in its overhaul manual.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Ignition compare
steps.prompt: Predict what supplies the initiating energy in a spark-ignition engine and in a compression-ignition engine, then toggle between them. Scrub through the end of compression and observe what enters the cylinder, when fuel is present, and what initiates combustion in each case.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 47-48, and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 23. The diesel cycle itself is taught in lesson 4; this step only contrasts the trigger. The animation is qualitative and assigns no unsourced compression ratios, injection pressures or temperatures.

mediaPlan.rationale: A controlled toggle keeps piston position constant while changing only the ignition mechanism.

steps.title: Aspiration: how the air gets in
steps.prompt:
Aspiration means how the air reaches the cylinders.

A naturally aspirated engine depends on atmospheric pressure to push the air-fuel mixture in. It is neither supercharged nor turbocharged.

A supercharger is an air compressor that raises the pressure of the air going to the cylinders. In an internally driven supercharger the compressor is driven by the engine itself, through a gear train from the crankshaft.

A turbocharger, which the handbook also calls an externally driven supercharger or turbosupercharger, takes its power from the exhaust: a small turbine in the exhaust drives the compressor on the same shaft.

The GTSIO-520-H is turbocharged and has an intake air intercooler. Lesson 11 explains how boost works.
steps.note: Naturally aspirated engine, supercharger, turbocharger and turbosupercharger as defined in the FAA handbook glossary; internally driven (gear train from the crankshaft) and externally driven (exhaust) superchargers, FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 134 to 135; the GTSIO-520-H intake air intercooler, overhaul manual difference data section C-3.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Carburetted or fuel-injected
steps.prompt:
A carburetor mixes the fuel into the air flowing through it. The float carburetor, the more common type, discharges fuel at a point of low pressure in the venturi, so the temperature drop from fuel vaporisation happens there and ice can form in the venturi and on the throttle valve. Pressure carburetors have mostly been replaced by fuel injection.

A fuel-injection system delivers metered fuel to the engine near the cylinders. The handbook lists its advantages over a carburetor: less danger of induction icing, because the temperature drop takes place in or near the cylinder; better acceleration; better fuel distribution between the cylinders; and better fuel economy.

The GTSIO-520-H has a Continental continuous-flow fuel-injection system.
steps.note: Carburetor types and icing, FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 90; the advantages of fuel injection over a carburetor system, PDF p. 103; the GTSIO-520-H's Continental continuous-flow fuel injection from the overhaul manual's difference data section C-3.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Direct drive or geared
steps.prompt:
In a direct-drive engine the propeller is mounted on the crankshaft and turns at engine speed. In a geared engine a reduction gear sits between them, so the propeller turns slower than the crankshaft.

Why bother? An engine develops more power at higher rpm, but when the blade tips approach the speed of sound the propeller's efficiency falls rapidly. Reduction gearing lets the engine run fast while the propeller turns at a speed where it works well.

The GTSIO-520-H has a propeller drive ratio of 0.667:1: the propeller turns at two-thirds of crankshaft speed. Its 2,275 propeller rpm therefore means the crankshaft is turning about 3,410 rpm.

The handbook describes spur planetary, bevel planetary and spur-and-pinion reduction gears.
steps.note: Reason for propeller reduction gearing and the three common types: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 44. The propeller drive ratio of 0.667:1 and 375 hp at 2,275 propeller rpm are from the GTSIO-520-H difference data section of the overhaul manual; 2,275 / 0.667 = 3,411 rpm is a calculation, not a figure in the manual.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Reading a model name
steps.prompt:
Manufacturers pack the classification into the model name. Take GTSIO-520-H.

Continental's own maintenance manual reads the code IO-520-X this way: I for fuel injection, O for horizontally opposed cylinders and 520 for the displacement in cubic inches. For this engine the arithmetic fits: six cylinders of 5.25 in bore and 4.00 in stroke displace 520 cubic inches.

The prefix reads as G for geared and TS for turbosupercharged, the two features the overhaul manual lists. The H marks the model within the series: this one makes 375 hp at 2,275 propeller rpm.

Letter codes differ between manufacturers, so check each in the maker's own key before relying on it.
steps.note: The IO-520 model code key is from Continental's IO-520 Permold Series Maintenance Manual, PDF p. 12. The G and TS reading is an interpretation: the GTSIO-520 manual describes the engine as geared and turbocharged (and, in its specification tables, turbosupercharged) but does not spell out the letters, and the handbook says turbosuperchargers are commonly called turbochargers. 375 hp at 2,275 propeller rpm and 520 cubic inches are from the -H difference data section.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Name every axis
steps.prompt:
Classification works on separate axes, and an engine sits at one point on each. Here is the GTSIO-520-H:

Cylinder arrangement: horizontally opposed. Cylinders: six. Cooling: air. Cycle: four-stroke. Ignition: spark. Aspiration: turbocharged. Fuelling: fuel-injected. Propeller drive: geared.

The axes are independent. A diesel can be two-stroke or four-stroke; a four-stroke can use spark or compression ignition; an opposed engine can be carburetted or injected.

When you describe an engine, name every axis that matters, as the manual does.
steps.note: Axes and values for the GTSIO-520-H from the manufacturer's overhaul manual (section I paragraph 1-2 and the -H difference data section); two magnetos and twelve spark plugs confirm spark ignition. The independence of the axes follows from the classifications themselves and is illustrated by FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 24 and 48 (diesels may be two-stroke or four-stroke).

mediaPlan.rationale: A verbal classification check prevents a common category error.

lessons.title: Cooling Methods
lessons.objective: Trace heat from the cylinder to the surrounding air in air-cooled, liquid-cooled and combined systems, identify the roles of fins, baffles, coolant, pump and radiator, and recognise why cooling condition and airflow path matter.
lessons.purpose: Explain the apparent paradox that although heat produces engine power, excessive heat must be removed.
outcomes: Explain why only part of the energy released by combustion becomes useful mechanical work.
Explain why an operating piston engine requires continuous heat rejection.
Describe the consequences of excessive engine temperature.
Describe the principle of air cooling.
Identify cooling fins, baffles, cowling and airflow passages.
Explain how airflow is directed around an air-cooled engine.
Describe the principle of liquid cooling.
Identify the principal components of a typical liquid-cooling system.
Describe the purpose and desirable characteristics of engine coolants.
Explain why water may be combined with additives or other coolant fluids.
Compare air and liquid cooling in terms of weight, complexity, temperature control, reliability, drag and maintenance.
Identify examples of engines that use each cooling method.
Explain why one cooling method may be selected over another for a particular aircraft application.
lessons.syllabusNote: Cooling methods and design are explicitly required under engine construction.
lessons.completionCriteria: Explain why only part of the fuel's energy becomes work and why the rest must be removed continuously; describe what too much heat does to combustion, to the parts and to lubrication, and why an engine can also run too cold; describe air cooling (fins, cowling, baffles, cowl flaps and the airflow path) and liquid cooling (jackets, pump, radiator, expansion tank); say what a coolant must do and why it is a mixture of water, glycol and additives; compare the two methods for weight, complexity, temperature control, drag and maintenance; name engines that use each; and argue which method suits a given aircraft - without treating a typical trait as universal.

steps.title: Where the energy goes
steps.prompt:
Burning fuel in a cylinder releases a great deal of heat, and the engine turns only part of it into work. The handbook puts the share that becomes power at roughly a quarter to a third. The rest has to go somewhere.

In a typical aircraft powerplant about half of the heat leaves with the exhaust, and the engine itself absorbs the other half. The circulating oil carries off part of that through the oil cooler, and the cooling system takes care of the rest.

Here is the paradox of this lesson: heat makes the power, yet heat must be removed continuously, for as long as the engine runs. One gallon of aviation gasoline holds enough heat to boil 75 gallons of water.

Predict the path unwanted heat takes from the cylinder metal to the air.
steps.note: About one-fourth of the heat released is changed into useful power, half goes out with the exhaust and the other half is absorbed by the engine, and a gallon of avgas could boil 75 gallons of water: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 278. Reciprocating engines about 34 percent thermally efficient: PDF p. 56 (the two figures are the handbook's own and differ by chapter, hence 'a quarter to a third'). This step frames the lesson using the instructor's learning outcomes; it is not an assessed fact.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short prediction prompt prepares learners to read the system diagrams that follow.

steps.title: When it gets too hot
steps.prompt:
The handbook gives three principal reasons why excessive heat is undesirable.

First, it changes how the charge burns. If the cylinder is too hot, the air-fuel mixture is preheated and burns before the planned moment. That premature combustion causes detonation and knocking.

Second, it weakens the engine's parts and shortens their lives.

Third, it impairs lubrication.

Unless most of the waste heat is rapidly removed, the cylinders can become hot enough to cause complete engine failure.

An engine can also run too cold. Fuel evaporation and distribution, and oil circulation, depend on the engine being kept at its best operating temperature. So the cooling system has to regulate heat as well as remove it.
steps.note: The three principal reasons excessive heat is undesirable, premature combustion and detonation, and the risk of engine failure: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 278. The risk of running too cold, and temperature control: PDF p. 279.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Air-cooled path
steps.prompt:
Trace heat from the cylinder wall and head into the fins, then into air directed through the cowling and baffles.

Identify how added fin area supports convection.
steps.alt: FAA cylinder baffle and deflector airflow diagram
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 24 and 278-282. Use the FAA cylinder-head/fin and cowling/baffle figures as the primary image source.

mediaPlan.rationale: A labelled source schematic clearly establishes the directed airflow path around the cylinder.

steps.title: Fins: more surface for the air
steps.prompt:
A cylinder on a large engine is roughly the size of a gallon jug. Its cooling fins increase its outer surface so that it presents a barrel-sized exterior to the cooling air. That increases the heat transfer by convection.

The fins are thin metal ribs on the cylinder barrel and head. The greatest improvement in air cooling came from making them thinner and deeper: modern fins taper from 0.090 inch at the base to 0.060 inch at the tip. More fin area is given where the metal is hottest, around the exhaust valve.

The head is cast aluminium alloy, which conducts heat rapidly and can be cast with deep, closely spaced fins.

If too much fin is broken off, the cylinder cannot cool properly and a hot spot develops. Cylinders are normally replaced if a specified number of square inches of fin is missing.
steps.note: Fin area and the gallon-jug comparison, and the effect of broken fins: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 278. Fin taper from 0.090 to 0.060 inch, extra fin area at the exhaust valve, aluminium alloy heads cast with deep, closely spaced fins: PDF p. 36.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: GTSIO cooling fins
steps.prompt: Inspect the GTSIO-520-H cylinder banks and locate the finned surfaces exposed to the installation airflow. Use the model to understand location and access, not to infer an exact heat-transfer rate.
steps.note: The GTSIO-520 overhaul manual identifies the basic engine as air cooled (PDF p. 13). The model is suitable for spatial inspection but is not a thermal simulation.

mediaPlan.rationale: The whole-engine model shows where the finned cylinders sit relative to the crankcase and installation airflow.

steps.title: Cowling, baffles and cowl flaps
steps.prompt:
Fins alone are not enough: the air must be made to go where the heat is.

The cowling streamlines the bulky engine, and it forms an envelope that forces air to pass around and between the cylinders. Baffles direct the air close around each cylinder so it cannot form hot pools of stagnant air while the main streams rush by unused. Blast tubes in the baffles aim jets of air at the rear spark plug elbows, to protect the ignition leads, and at accessories such as the alternator and starter.

Only about 15 to 30 percent of the air approaching the nacelle enters the cowling; the rest flows over the outside.

Cowl flaps at the exit control the flow. Opened, they let more air through and the engine cools; closed, it warms. Opened, they also add drag.
steps.note: Cowling, baffles, blast tubes and the 15 to 30 percent of ram air that enters the cowling: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 278 and 280. Cowl flaps change the exit area and so the temperature, and add drag when extended: PDF pp. 279 and 280.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Airflow condition
steps.prompt: Change the qualitative inputs: low or high cooling airflow, fins clear or obstructed, baffles sealed or leaking. Observe how each condition changes the intended airflow path and relative cooling margin.
steps.note: Documented relationships from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 278-282. The planned output will use relative labels only; it will not calculate cylinder-head temperature or declare an engine airworthy.

mediaPlan.rationale: Learner-selected airflow and obstruction states make the role of fins and baffles causal rather than merely labelled.

steps.title: Inspection connection
steps.prompt:
Cooling fins and baffles work as a system.

Damaged or obstructed fins reduce heat-transfer area. Missing or poor-fitting baffles let cooling air bypass the surfaces that need it.

Actual acceptance limits and corrective action come from the applicable maintenance data.
steps.note: Documented general inspection relationship from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 282. This is a recognition lesson, not an approval-to-service procedure.

mediaPlan.rationale: The final step connects theory to maintenance judgment while preserving the manual boundary.

steps.title: Liquid-cooled path
steps.prompt:
In a liquid-cooled engine, passages called water jackets surround the cylinders. A liquid coolant circulates through them and carries the excess heat away. The coolant then passes through a radiator, a heat exchanger in the airstream, which gives the heat to the air.

So the heat takes one more step than in an air-cooled engine: cylinder metal, coolant, radiator, air. A pump keeps the coolant moving.

The price is weight: the coolant, radiator, pump and tubing all have to be carried. In return, liquid cooling allows high power to be obtained safely, and it cools more evenly.

Most piston aircraft engines are air cooled. Liquid cooling appears in a few high-power engines and some diesels.
steps.note: Water jackets, coolant and radiator, and that some diesel liquid-cooled engines are available for light aircraft: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 278. Added weight of coolant, radiator and tubing, and that liquid cooling allows high power safely: PDF p. 24, and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 23. More uniform, controlled cooling is the course slides' claim (slide 106).

mediaPlan.rationale: The system path is short enough to establish in text before a comparison graphic.

steps.title: The parts of a liquid system
steps.prompt:
Take the Rotax 914 as an example. Its cooling system for the cylinder heads is a closed circuit.

A water pump, driven from the camshaft, pushes coolant from the radiator to the cylinder heads. From the top of the heads it passes to an expansion tank. The radiator sits below engine level, so the tank on top of the engine gives the coolant room to expand.

The tank has a pressure cap with an excess-pressure valve and a return valve. As the coolant warms, the valve opens and coolant flows to a transparent overflow bottle. When it cools, the coolant is sucked back. Temperature probes in the cylinder heads read the hottest point.

So the parts are: jackets or head passages, pump, radiator, expansion tank and cap, overflow bottle, hoses and temperature sensors.
steps.note: The Rotax 914 cooling circuit (pump driven from the camshaft, radiator, cylinder heads, expansion tank with pressure cap, overflow bottle, temperature probes): FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 439 and Figure 11-7. This is an example of one system, not a claim about every liquid-cooled engine.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: What a coolant must do
steps.prompt:
A coolant has one job: to carry heat from the hot metal to the radiator. To do that in an engine it must meet several demands at once.

It must carry a lot of heat for its volume, which favours a liquid with a high specific heat. It must stay liquid across the whole range of temperatures the engine meets, neither freezing on a cold night nor boiling in a hot cylinder head. And it must protect the metals it touches, aluminium among them, from corrosion.

No single liquid does all of this. Water carries heat very well but freezes, boils and corrodes. So engine coolants are mixtures.
steps.note: The coolant's function (protecting the cylinder heads from over-temperature by heat dissipation, with additives against corrosion and freezing): Rotax SI-912-016R9, section 4.1. The requirements of range of temperature, heat capacity and corrosion protection are drawn from Rotax section 4 and the Wikipedia Antifreeze article. Checked 13 October 2026.

mediaPlan.rationale: A simple three-row table of demands (carry heat, stay liquid, protect metal) against water, glycol and a mixture makes the compromise visible.
mediaPlan.assetBrief: A labelled comparison with three demands (carry heat, stay liquid, resist corrosion) and three columns: water, ethylene glycol, a 50/50 mixture. Qualitative marks only, no invented numbers.

steps.title: Why water, glycol and additives
steps.prompt:
Water is the base of a coolant: cheap, harmless and good at carrying heat. On its own it has three faults. It freezes, and the expanding ice can burst an engine. It boils, and steam pockets in the jackets make hot spots. And it promotes corrosion between the different metals in the system.

Ethylene glycol cures the first two: it lowers the freezing point and raises the boiling point. But it carries less heat than water, so the mix is a compromise. Rotax allows ethylene glycol with about 50 percent water, which keeps the higher heat capacity but can boil as low as 120 degrees C, so it sets a temperature limit.

Additives protect the metals from corrosion. They are used up, so the coolant is replaced on schedule.

Rotax also allows a waterless coolant: it will not boil, but its lower heat capacity means slightly higher running temperatures.
steps.note: The faults of pure water, the effect of glycol on freezing and boiling points, its lower heat capacity, and the depletion of corrosion inhibitors: Wikipedia, Antifreeze. The 50 percent mix, the 120 degrees C boiling warning, the waterless coolant and its trade-off: Rotax SI-912-016R9, section 4. The FAA glossary calls ethylene glycol a permanent antifreeze (PDF p. 469). Checked 13 October 2026.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Combined cooling
steps.prompt: Study an example in which liquid cools the cylinder heads while air cools the cylinder barrels. Follow each heat path separately rather than labelling the whole engine as only air cooled or only liquid cooled.
steps.alt: Rotax 914 cooling system diagram: coolant circulates through the cylinder heads, expansion tank, radiator and overflow bottle, while the cylinders are cooled by ram air
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 440 (Figure 11-7 and its text): the Rotax 914 uses liquid cooling of the cylinder heads and ram-air cooling of the cylinders. The figure draws the liquid circuit only; the air path is in the text. Use it as an example, not as a claim about the GTSIO-520.

mediaPlan.rationale: A real combined-system schematic prevents the false assumption that cooling methods are always all-or-nothing.

steps.title: Air or liquid: the comparison
steps.prompt:
Compare the two methods point by point. These are typical differences, not rules.

Weight: liquid cooling adds coolant, radiator, pump and tubing. Air cooling needs only fins, cowling and baffles.

Complexity and reliability: a liquid system has more parts and more places to fail, such as leaks and pump problems. An air-cooled engine is simpler.

Temperature control: liquid cooling is more uniform and controlled. Air cooling is less even and depends on airflow, which obstruction or extreme ambient temperature can upset.

Drag: both put something in the airstream. Opened cowl flaps add drag to an air-cooled engine; a liquid-cooled one needs a radiator in the airstream.

Maintenance: air cooling needs less. Liquid cooling means coolant to check, change and keep free of leaks.
steps.note: Weight, complexity, temperature control and maintenance as the course slides give them (slides 106 and 107, the instructor's deck: these are generalisations, not measured data); added weight of coolant, radiator and tubing, and a radiator placed in the airstream: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 24; cowl flaps adding drag: PDF p. 279.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Engines and their cooling
steps.prompt:
Air cooled: the GTSIO-520-H and IO-520 of this course; the Lycoming O-320 and Continental O-200 of the flight schools; the radials, such as the Wright Whirlwind that carried the Spirit of St. Louis across the Atlantic.

Liquid cooled: the Rolls-Royce Merlin, in its Packard-built form a V-12 of 1,490 hp, and some modern diesels.

Both: the Rotax 912 and 914, with liquid-cooled cylinder heads and ram-air-cooled cylinders.

So the method follows the job. Engines of very different eras and powers are found in each group.
steps.note: GTSIO-520 and IO-520 air cooled: the manufacturers' manuals; Lycoming O-320 and Continental O-200: course slide 107; Spirit of St. Louis air-cooled Wright J-5C Whirlwind: This Day in Aviation; Packard Merlin V-1650-7 liquid cooled, V-12, 1,490 hp: Smithsonian record; some diesel engines liquid cooled: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 278; Rotax 912/914: Rotax SI-912-016R9 and FAA PDF p. 439.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Choosing a cooling method
steps.prompt:
There is no best cooling method, only the best for the job. Ask what the aircraft needs.

A flight-school trainer or a bush plane wants light weight, few parts and cheap upkeep, and its engine sits out in the airstream anyway. Air cooling suits it, which is why most general aviation engines are air cooled.

An engine pushed to high power, where air cooling would struggle to hold temperatures in check, may justify the weight and complexity of liquid cooling. The wartime V-12s are the classic case.

Many designs compromise. The Rotax 914 liquid cools only the hot cylinder heads and lets ram air cool the rest.

Engineers weigh power, weight, complexity, maintenance and the installation, and the answer differs from aircraft to aircraft.
steps.note: That the cooling method depends on the application and aircraft type, and that most general aviation engines are air cooled, with liquid cooling supporting higher power: course slides 106 to 108 (instructor deck) and FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 24. The Rotax 914 compromise: FAA PDF p. 439 and Rotax SI-912-016R9. The wartime V-12 is illustrated by the Merlin record.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

lessons.title: Parts and Construction
lessons.objective: Name the major structural and power-section parts of a piston engine - crankcase sections, crankshaft, connecting rods, pistons, rings and pins, cylinders, bearings, propeller shaft and mounts - state what each does and what it is made of, and recognise how the GTSIO-520-H's construction differs from a direct-drive engine such as the IO-520.
lessons.purpose: Build a physical understanding of what the piston engine is made from and why its components take the forms they do.

Explain the main mechanical and thermal loads experienced by important engine parts.
