steps.title: The basic parts
steps.prompt:
Every piston engine is built from the same core parts: a crankcase, cylinders, pistons, connecting rods, a crankshaft, and valves with their operating mechanism.

Before opening them up, predict which part carries the whole engine's load and keeps the crankshaft in alignment.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 26 (major components of a reciprocating engine; the crankcase must be rigid enough to prevent misalignment of the crankshaft and its bearings).

mediaPlan.rationale: A prediction prompt frames the walk through the components.

steps.title: Stationary or moving?
steps.prompt:
Sort the core parts into two groups.

Stationary parts do not move relative to the engine as a whole: the crankcase and its sections, the cylinders and heads, and the mounting lugs. They hold everything in place and take the loads.

Moving parts do the work: the pistons and rings, the piston pins, the connecting rods, the crankshaft, the valves and their operating mechanism, and the gears and shafts that drive the accessories and the propeller.

Where a moving part meets a stationary one there is a bearing or a sliding surface: the crankshaft turns in its main bearings in the crankcase, and the piston slides in the cylinder.

The sorting is relative. In a rotary engine the crankshaft is fixed and the crankcase and cylinders revolve.
steps.note: A working definition for this course, consistent with common engineering usage; the handbook does not use these two labels. The basic major components of a reciprocating engine: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 26. The rotary radial engine, whose crankshaft is fixed while the propeller, crankcase and cylinders revolve: FAA handbook glossary, and lesson 5.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: The crankcase
steps.prompt: The crankcase is the foundation. It holds the crankshaft bearings, supports the cylinders and carries the mounting lugs, so it must stay rigid under bending and vibration. It is normally cast or forged aluminium alloy. On the GTSIO-520-H, two aluminium alloy castings, left and right, are joined along the vertical centre plane.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 26-27, EASA Module 16, PDF p. 51, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, Section III paragraph 3-1b (PDF p. 16). The whole-engine mesh is a teaching reconstruction and keeps its modelling-status disclosure.

mediaPlan.rationale: The whole-engine model shows the two crankcase halves with the cylinders on each side.

steps.title: Sections of the case
steps.prompt: Find the two crankcase halves, the accessory (rear) case and the oil sump. The nose section at the front houses the propeller shaft, or the reduction gears on a geared engine, while the rear section carries the magnetos, pumps, starter and alternator.
steps.alt: FAA exploded view of an opposed engine showing the crankcase halves, accessory case, oil sump, crankshaft, camshaft, cylinder and accessories
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 26-28 (nose section, accessory section, Figure 1-6). Sump construction differs by engine: the IO-520 manual notes cast or stamped aluminium sumps.

mediaPlan.rationale: The FAA exploded view names every major case section and accessory in one labelled figure.

steps.title: The crankshaft
steps.prompt:
The crankshaft is the engine's backbone: a forged alloy steel shaft with a throw for each cylinder. A throw is two crank cheeks and a crankpin, and the journals turn in the main bearings.

The crankpin is usually hollow, which saves weight and carries oil. The GTSIO-520-H's six-throw shaft has nitrided journals and crankpins, and counterweights that oscillate on pins to damp torsional vibration.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 29-30, EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 53-55, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, Section III paragraph 3-1e (PDF pp. 16-17). The model shows one throw of the detailed operating cylinder.

mediaPlan.rationale: Spotlighting one crank throw on the operating-cylinder model shows cheeks, crankpin and journal in place.

steps.title: Connecting rods
steps.prompt:
The connecting rod links the piston to the crankpin. It must stay rigid under load yet be light enough to limit inertia forces at each stroke end.

Opposed and inline engines use plain rods, with a cap and two-piece bearing at the crankpin end and a bushing at the piston end. Rods go back in the same cylinder and position. The GTSIO-520-H uses I-beam rods with split bronze piston-pin bushings.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 30-32, EASA Module 16, PDF p. 66, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, paragraph 3-1f (PDF p. 17): I-beam rods, two identical precision inserts at the crankpin end, weight variation limited to 1/2 ounce in a bay.

mediaPlan.rationale: The rod, cap, bearing halves, bolts and small-end bushing are spotlighted together.

steps.title: Other rod types
steps.prompt: Radial engines use a master rod with articulated rods, and V engines use fork-and-blade rods. Match the four connecting-rod types in the figure - plain, fork-and-blade, master-and-articulated, and split-type - to the engine layouts that use them.
steps.alt: FAA diagram of connecting rod assemblies: solid master rod with articulated rod, fork-and-blade rod, plain rod and split-type master rod
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 30-32 (four types of connecting-rod assembly; Figure 1-11) and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 66.

mediaPlan.rationale: The FAA figure shows all four rod assemblies side by side with their parts labelled.

steps.title: Piston and pin
steps.prompt: The piston is the moving wall of the combustion chamber: an aluminium alloy forging with ring grooves, heavy pin bosses and inner ribs that help oil carry heat away. The full-floating piston pin turns freely in both the piston and the rod, and soft aluminium end plugs stop it scoring the cylinder wall.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 33-34, EASA Module 16, PDF p. 63, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, paragraph 3-1g (PDF p. 17): aluminium alloy pistons with solid skirts, full-floating ground steel pins with forged-in aluminium plugs.

mediaPlan.rationale: The piston body, pin and end plugs are spotlighted with the cylinder ghosted around them.

steps.title: Piston rings
steps.prompt:
Rings seal the combustion gas and control the oil. Compression rings, usually two, sit nearest the crown; oil control rings scrape surplus oil back to the crankcase. Most rings are gray cast iron, and chrome rings belong only with steel cylinder walls.

This piston has two compression rings, a slotted oil-control ring and an oil scraper. The GTSIO-520 series has used a four-ring piston since 1975, and piston types must not be intermixed.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 34-35, EASA Module 16, PDF p. 65, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, paragraph 3-1g (PDF p. 17): four-ring piston since 1975, replacing the five-ring model; some pistons have a cast steel top-groove insert and the weight difference means they are not to be intermixed.

mediaPlan.rationale: The four rings are spotlighted so each can be named by its job.

steps.title: The cylinder
steps.prompt:
Each cylinder is two parts: a light aluminium alloy head with deep cooling fins, and a steel barrel nitrided inside to resist wear.

The head is heated and screwed onto the chilled barrel, so as they equalise they lock into a gastight shrink joint. The head also carries the valve seats and guides and the spark plug openings.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 35-36, EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 56-57, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, paragraph 3-1c (PDF p. 16): heads heated, seats and guides installed, then screwed and shrunk onto the steel barrel; 18 mm helical-coil spark plug inserts.

mediaPlan.rationale: The barrel and head are spotlighted as one assembly.

steps.title: Bearings
steps.prompt:
Bearings support moving parts with little friction and carry radial loads, thrust loads, or both.

Plain bearings of soft alloys serve the crankshaft, camshaft and connecting rods. Deep-groove ball bearings carry radial and thrust loads; straight roller bearings carry radial load only. The GTSIO-520-H's crankshaft rides in precision steel-backed, lead-alloy-lined main bearing inserts.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 43-44 (radial and thrust loads; plain, ball and roller bearings), and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, paragraph 3-1b (PDF p. 16).

mediaPlan.rationale: A short classification by load type needs no visual.

steps.title: Propeller shaft and reduction gears
steps.prompt:
The propeller shaft is tapered, splined or flanged; on small direct-drive engines it is just an extension of the crankshaft.

Powerful engines add reduction gears so the crankshaft can turn fast while the propeller turns slower, before its tip speed nears the speed of sound. Name the three common types in the figure.

The GTSIO-520-H is geared: a quill shaft carries torque to a reduction gear that drives the flanged propeller shaft at 0.667:1.
steps.alt: FAA diagram of propeller reduction gears: spur planetary, bevel planetary, and spur and pinion
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 44-45, EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 67-70, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual (PDF pp. 16-17 for the quill shaft and reduction gear; PDF p. 152 for the 0.667:1 propeller drive ratio).

mediaPlan.rationale: The FAA figure shows the three reduction-gear arrangements with their parts named.

steps.title: Loads on the parts
steps.prompt:
Each part has its own loads, and the loads explain its shape.

Crankcase: bending that changes continuously in direction and size, and the tremendous force trying to pull each cylinder off its pad. At the nose of a geared engine there are also propeller thrust and gyroscopic forces in manoeuvres.

Crankshaft: it takes most of the forces the engine develops, and the vibration of the power impulses.

Connecting rod: the push of the piston, and the inertia forces each time rod and piston stop, change direction and start again.

Piston: the gas load. At maximum power the push can exceed 15 tons, from gas at 3,000 to 4,000 degrees F.

Cylinder head and valves: extreme heat. Exhaust valves run hotter than intake valves.
steps.note: Crankcase loads, cylinder pull-off, bending and nose loads: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 26. Crankshaft takes most of the forces: PDF p. 28. Rod inertia forces: PDF p. 29. Cylinder heads at extreme temperatures: PDF p. 35. Intake valves cooler than exhaust valves: PDF p. 38. The force on the piston (more than 15 tons) and the burning-gas temperature (3,000 to 4,000 degrees F): PDF p. 48.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Materials and why
steps.prompt:
Each material is a compromise among strength, mass, wear, heat flow and cost.

Crankcase: cast or forged aluminium alloy, light and strong. Cylinder head: aluminium alloy, a good conductor of heat and light. Barrel: forged steel, hardened inside against wear.

Piston: forged aluminium alloy, light to keep inertia low. Rings: gray cast iron.

Crankshaft: forged chromium-nickel-molybdenum steel for strength, with journals and crankpins nitrided against wear.

Connecting rods: forged steel alloy, rigid yet light.

Bearings: soft non-ferrous alloys such as bronze, silver and lead-tin, which give way before the shaft does.

Valves: chromic-nickel steel for the cooler intake; nichrome, silchrome or cobalt-chromium steel for the exhaust, some with sodium in the stem to carry heat away.
steps.note: Crankcase, crankshaft, rods, pistons, cylinder heads, valves (including sodium-filled stems), bearings: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 26 to 29, 33, 35, 38 and 43; rings of gray cast iron, the steel barrel and the soft bearing alloys also appear in the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual and EASA Module 16. Typical materials, not rules for every engine.

mediaPlan.rationale: A single table of part, material and the reason for choosing it makes the compromise easy to compare.
mediaPlan.assetBrief: A labelled table: part, typical material, and one reason (strength, mass, wear, heat transfer). Drawn from the handbook; no invented properties.

steps.title: Engine mounts
steps.prompt:
The engine hangs from the airframe on an engine mount: a steel-tube structure with a ring that surrounds the engine near its point of balance.

Dynafocal mounts angle their pads toward the engine's centre of gravity. Rubber-and-steel shock mounts let the engine move a little while metal snubbers limit extreme movement. Rubber ages, so hoses and controls must be able to flex.
steps.alt: Photograph of an engine mounting ring on a light aircraft firewall with four dynamic mount fittings
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 27 and 343-344 (mounting lugs, mount ring, dynafocal and shock mounts), and EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 53 and 275-276 (rubber mounts, relative motion between engine and airframe).

mediaPlan.rationale: A photograph of a real mounting ring shows the fittings that hold the dynamic mounts.

steps.title: How the mount carries the load
steps.prompt:
Follow the load from the engine to the airframe.

The mounting lugs on the crankcase attach to the engine mount ring. The ring is part of a welded steel-tube structure with bracing members, and that structure passes the loads on to the wing nacelle or firewall. It must support the whole powerplant, including the propeller, with ample strength for rapid manoeuvres.

Special heat-treated steel bolts alone support the weight of the engine and the stresses of engine and propeller in flight. On the ground the upper bolts carry the weight; in flight a torsional stress is added to all of them.

The shock mounts do a second job: the rubber deforms slightly, so vibration is damped before it reaches the airframe.
steps.note: Mounting lugs and the strength of the mounting arrangement: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 27. Mount structure, mounting ring, heat-treated bolts, upper bolts and in-flight torsion, shock mounts and snubbers: PDF p. 344. Vibration isolation by resilient material: PDF p. 344 and EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 275 to 276.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Find the main parts
steps.prompt:
Now find the main parts on the whole GTSIO-520-H.

The highlighted parts are the crankcase with its mounting lugs, the crankshaft inside it, and the propeller reduction drive at the front.

Orbit the model. Where would the moving parts of a cylinder sit? Which part would the engine mount grip?
steps.note: The whole-engine model keeps its modelling-status disclosure: it is a teaching reconstruction, so use it to find parts and their relations, not to measure. The parts named are components of the engine contract (crankcase-and-mounts, crankshaft, propeller-reduction-drive).

mediaPlan.rationale: Spotlighting the crankcase, crankshaft and reduction drive on the whole-engine model lets the learner locate them on the real arrangement.

steps.title: Direct or geared?
steps.prompt: Compare the GTSIO-520-H with the IO-520 part by part. Find what is identical and what differs. Which difference changes how the propeller is attached to the engine?
steps.note: GTSIO-520-H from its overhaul manual, Section III (PDF pp. 16-17) and Chapter C-3 (PDF p. 152). IO-520 from its overhaul manual, paragraphs 2-3 to 2-9. The IO-520 is a different engine, used for comparison only.

mediaPlan.rationale: A side-by-side table makes identical and differing construction obvious at a glance.

lessons.title: Two-stroke cycle
lessons.objective: Explain how a two-stroke engine completes the operating cycle in one crankshaft revolution by combining intake and exhaust in the same stroke, and where it is used in aircraft.
lessons.completionCriteria: State that a two-stroke cycle completes in one crankshaft revolution, name the functions that share a stroke, and give one advantage and one disadvantage compared with the four-stroke cycle.

steps.title: One revolution, one cycle
steps.prompt: A four-stroke engine needs two crankshaft revolutions for one cycle. A two-stroke engine needs only one upstroke and one downstroke, so it completes the operating cycle in a single revolution and every cylinder fires once per revolution. Predict how that is possible: what has to happen to the intake and exhaust functions?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48: two upstroke-and-downstroke pairs are not needed; the cycle completes in one revolution and 'the intake and exhaust functions are accomplished during the same stroke'. That every cylinder fires once per revolution follows from one cycle per revolution.

mediaPlan.rationale: A prediction prompt frames the port-timing interactive that follows.

steps.title: Port timing
steps.prompt: Step through one crankshaft revolution of a two-stroke cycle. Observe how intake and exhaust functions share part of the same piston movement, rather than occupying four separate strokes.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48. The FAA text states that a two-stroke cycle completes in one crankshaft revolution and combines intake and exhaust functions during the same stroke.

mediaPlan.rationale: Port opening and closing are time relationships; a learner-controlled phase animation is clearer than a single still.

steps.title: Where two-strokes fly
steps.prompt: The two-stroke engine has re-emerged in ultra-light, light sport and many experimental aircraft. These engines can be air or water cooled and generally need a gear reduction housing between engine and propeller. The course's comparison lists a power stroke every revolution, light and simple construction (no valves) and compact size as advantages, against lower fuel efficiency, shorter time between overhauls, more emissions and poorer scavenging.
steps.note: Aircraft use, cooling and gear reduction documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48. The advantages and disadvantages list is the course deck, slides 65 and 67 (tier 4); it is not in the FAA or EASA text.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short comparison list needs no visual.

lessons.title: Rotary (Wankel) cycle
lessons.objective: Describe how a rotary engine produces the four cycle events in chambers around a three-sided rotor instead of in a reciprocating piston engine's cylinders.
lessons.completionCriteria: Describe the rotor and housing, name the four events that occur in the chambers, and give one advantage and one disadvantage of the rotary engine.

steps.title: A rotor instead of a piston
steps.prompt: A rotary (Wankel) engine has no reciprocating piston. A three-sided rotor turns inside an elliptical housing, and the four events of the cycle take place in the changing chambers between rotor and housing. These engines can have one rotor or several, can be air or water cooled, are used mostly in experimental and light aircraft, and have very low vibration.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48, and EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 22-23.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short orientation before the source figure.

steps.title: Chambers around the rotor
steps.prompt: Trace how the three-sided rotor creates changing chambers for intake, compression, combustion/expansion and exhaust while producing rotary output.
steps.alt: EASA diagram showing intake, compression, power and exhaust chambers in a rotary engine
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48, and EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 22-23. Use the source figure first. A short licensed or self-authored motion clip is optional only if the static chamber sequence proves insufficient in review.

mediaPlan.rationale: The EASA source already supplies the required rotor, housing and phase geometry; a generated technical image would add avoidable fidelity risk.

steps.title: Rotary trade-offs
steps.prompt: The course lists the strengths of the Wankel as very compact and light, few moving parts and so low vibration, and no valves. Against that come lower thermal efficiency from the shape of the combustion chamber, poor emissions control, faster apex-seal wear, higher fuel and oil consumption, and limited certification and support in aviation.
steps.note: Advantages and disadvantages are the course deck, slide 71 (tier 4); they are not in the FAA or EASA text.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short comparison list needs no visual.

checks.question: Put the four strokes in operating order.
checks.hint: Begin with the stroke that admits the fresh charge.
checks.rationale: A four-stroke cycle repeats intake, compression, power and exhaust over two crankshaft revolutions.

checks.question: What initiates combustion in the diesel cycle described by the FAA and EASA sources?
checks.hint: Consider what happens to air temperature during high compression.
answers: An electric spark across a plug gap
High temperature produced by compressing air before fuel injection
A continuously burning flame in the exhaust
checks.rationale: The cylinder compresses air to high pressure and temperature, then injected fuel ignites in that hot compressed air.

checks.question: Put the four processes of the ideal Otto cycle in order.
checks.hint: Start with the piston moving toward top dead centre.
checks.rationale: The ideal Otto cycle compresses the charge, adds heat at constant volume, expands it, then rejects heat at constant volume.

checks.question: How does heat addition in the ideal Diesel cycle differ from the ideal Otto cycle?
checks.hint: Compare the heat-addition line on the two diagrams.
answers: Diesel adds heat at constant pressure; Otto adds it at constant volume
Diesel adds no heat; Otto adds heat with a spark
Both add heat at constant volume, but Diesel does it more slowly
checks.rationale: Fuel burns as it is injected in the diesel cycle, so heat is added at roughly constant pressure; the ideal Otto cycle adds it instantly at constant volume.

checks.question: What is valve overlap?
checks.hint: Look for the shaded interval around TDC on the timing chart.
answers: Both valves off their seats at the same time around TDC, between the exhaust and intake strokes
The intake valve staying open throughout the compression stroke
The time a valve takes to open fully
checks.rationale: The intake valve opens before TDC (lead) and the exhaust valve closes after TDC (lag), so both are open briefly, which aids cooling, charging and scavenging.

checks.question: The intake valve opening before TDC on the exhaust stroke is called:
checks.hint: The valve acts before the piston reaches the end of the stroke.
answers: Valve lead
Valve lag
Valve clearance
checks.rationale: Opening a valve before its stroke begins is valve lead; closing it after its stroke ends is valve lag.

checks.question: Why is the practical pressure-volume diagram rounder than the ideal Otto diagram?
checks.hint: Think about what the ideal cycle assumes happens instantly.
answers: Burning takes time and the valves open early and close late
A real engine has no compression stroke
The piston stops for a moment at TDC in a real engine
checks.rationale: The ideal cycle assumes instant heat addition and instant valve action; real burning and valve events take crank angle, and heat is lost to the walls.

checks.question: Which statement describes a heat engine?
checks.hint: Follow the energy: where does it start, what does it become, and what happens to the part that is not used?
answers: It takes in heat from a hot source, turns part of it into work and rejects the rest to something cooler
It turns all the heat it receives into work
It makes heat from nothing
It moves heat from a cold place to a hot place without any work
checks.rationale: A heat engine converts part of the heat it takes in into work and must discard the remainder as heat. A piston engine does this with the burning charge as the hot source.

checks.question: A heat engine takes in 500 J of heat and rejects 330 J to the surroundings. What is its thermal efficiency, as a percentage?
checks.hint: The work is the heat in minus the heat rejected. Efficiency is the work divided by the heat in.
checks.rationale: Work = 500 - 330 = 170 J. Efficiency = 170 / 500 = 0.34, or 34 percent. The remaining 330 J leaves as heat, in a piston engine mostly through the exhaust and the cooling.

checks.question: Match each process to what stays fixed.
checks.hint: The names come from Greek: iso- means equal, and adiabatic means no passing through.

pairs.right: No heat passes into or out of the gas

checks.rationale: Constant volume, constant pressure, constant temperature and no heat exchange are the four basic processes from which the engine cycles are built.

checks.question: On a pressure-volume diagram of an engine cycle, what does the area enclosed by the loop represent?
checks.hint: Think of the area under a path as the work done, and subtract the work that must be put back in.
answers: The net work done by the gas in one cycle
The heat rejected in one cycle
The highest pressure in the cycle
The time one cycle takes
checks.rationale: The area under each path is work. Around a full loop the work done on expansion exceeds the work needed to compress, and the enclosed area is the difference: the net work of the cycle.

checks.question: A Carnot engine works between a hot source at 1,000 K and a cold sink at 300 K. What is its efficiency, as a percentage?
checks.hint: Use efficiency = 1 - (cold / hot), with both temperatures in kelvin.
checks.rationale: 1 - 300 / 1,000 = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7, or 70 percent. No real engine between those two temperatures can do better, and real engines fall below it.

checks.question: What does the Carnot efficiency tell you about a real engine?
checks.hint: It is a limit, not a prediction. Which way does a real engine lie from it?
answers: It is the highest efficiency any engine could have between the same two temperatures; a real engine is lower
It is the efficiency every real engine achieves
It is the lowest efficiency a real engine can have
It only applies to gas turbines
checks.rationale: Carnot efficiency is an upper bound set by the two temperatures. Friction, heat losses and non-ideal combustion keep real engines below it.

checks.question: The spark fires before TDC, while the piston is still on its compression stroke. What does this show about strokes and events?
checks.hint: A stroke describes the piston. An event describes what happens to the charge. Which one starts early here?
answers: Events (what happens to the charge) can begin before the stroke that is named after them
The piston has changed direction early
The cycle has skipped a stroke
Ignition belongs to the exhaust stroke
checks.rationale: Strokes are the piston's motion and events are what happens to the charge. The two overlap: ignition happens before TDC and burning carries on into the power stroke.

checks.question: A piston starts the intake stroke at TDC. Through how many degrees of crankshaft rotation has it turned when it finishes the power stroke?
checks.hint: Each stroke is 180 degrees. Count the strokes up to the end of the power stroke: intake, compression, power.
checks.rationale: Intake 0 to 180, compression 180 to 360, power 360 to 540. The exhaust stroke then runs from 540 to 720 degrees, completing two turns of the crankshaft.

checks.question: How often does each cylinder of a two-stroke engine deliver a power stroke?
checks.hint: Compare with the four-stroke, which fires once in two revolutions.
answers: Once in every revolution of the crankshaft
Once in every two revolutions
Once in every four revolutions
Twice in every revolution
checks.rationale: A two-stroke completes the operating cycle in one revolution, with intake and exhaust in the same stroke, so each cylinder has a power stroke every turn. A four-stroke fires once in two turns.

checks.question: Put the four events of the Brayton cycle in the order the air meets them.
checks.hint: Follow a particle of air through a gas turbine from the front to the back.
checks.rationale: The handbook lists the four events of the gas turbine as intake, compression, expansion (which includes the power) and exhaust. They go on continuously, each in a different part of the engine.

checks.question: Which description identifies a radial engine arrangement?
checks.hint: Think about the view from the propeller end.
answers: One straight cylinder bank
Two banks directly opposite each other
One or more rows of cylinders around a central crankcase
checks.rationale: A radial engine arranges its cylinders in one or more rows around a central crankcase.

checks.question: How does the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual describe the basic engine's cylinder arrangement?
checks.hint: The two banks face each other across the crankcase.
answers: Six-cylinder horizontally opposed
Nine-cylinder radial
Twelve-cylinder V-type
checks.rationale: The manual describes the basic GTSIO-520 engine as a six-cylinder horizontally opposed engine.

checks.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes spark ignition from compression ignition?
checks.hint: Focus on what starts combustion, not the number of strokes.
answers: Spark ignition uses an electric spark; compression ignition relies on the temperature of highly compressed air
Spark ignition is always two-stroke; compression ignition is always four-stroke
Spark ignition uses a turbocharger; compression ignition cannot
checks.rationale: The ignition methods differ in the combustion trigger. Stroke cycle and aspiration are separate classifications.

checks.question: How are the GTSIO-520-H's cylinders numbered?
checks.hint: Left and right are taken as seen from the accessory end.
answers: From the rear, with odd numbers on the right and even numbers on the left
From the front, filling one bank before the other
Clockwise from the top cylinder
checks.rationale: The overhaul manual numbers the cylinders starting from the rear, odd on the right and even on the left; other manufacturers may number from the front, so the manual always decides.

checks.question: Put the GTSIO-520-H cylinders in firing order.
checks.hint: Cylinder 1 fires first; the order is in the manual's ignition system table.
checks.rationale: The GTSIO-520-H fires 1-4-5-2-3-6; the similar IO-520 fires 1-6-3-2-5-4, so the order must come from the engine's own manual.

checks.question: Match each engine to its cylinder arrangement.
checks.hint: Picture each engine from the front: where are its cylinders?

pairs.right: Rotary (the cylinders revolve with the propeller)

checks.rationale: The GTSIO-520 has two banks opposite each other. The V-1710 is the handbook's example of a V-type, the R-3350 a radial, and the Gnome a rotary whose crankshaft is fixed while the cylinders turn.

checks.question: Six cylinders each have a 5.25 in bore and a 4.00 in stroke. What is the engine's total displacement, in cubic inches?
checks.hint: The swept volume of one cylinder is 0.7854 x bore squared x stroke. Multiply by the number of cylinders.
checks.rationale: 0.7854 x 5.25 x 5.25 x 4.00 = 86.6 cubic inches per cylinder, and six cylinders give about 519.5, which the manual rounds to 520.

checks.question: Why must the cylinders of an engine be numbered?
checks.hint: Think of a technician with a logbook, a gauge reading and a manual.
answers: So that every record, reading and procedure can refer to the same cylinder
Because the cylinders differ in size
Because the firing order is always 1-2-3-4-5-6
Because numbering makes the engine run smoother
checks.rationale: The numbering gives each cylinder a name shared by the manuals, logbooks and gauges, and a fixed starting point for procedures such as magneto timing.

checks.question: What is the main problem with liquid cooling in an aircraft engine?
checks.hint: Think of everything that has to be carried besides the engine.
answers: The added weight of the coolant, radiator and tubing
It cannot cool a high-power engine
It makes the engine overheat
It needs fins on the cylinders
checks.rationale: The handbook names the added weight of coolant, heat exchanger and tubing as the main problem, though liquid cooling does allow high power to be obtained safely.

checks.question: What drives the compressor of a turbocharger?
checks.hint: The name says what it does with the engine's waste.
answers: A turbine turned by the exhaust gases
A gear train from the crankshaft
An electric motor
The ram air in the intake
checks.rationale: A turbocharger takes its power from the exhaust. An internally driven supercharger is driven by a gear train from the crankshaft.

checks.question: Match each part of an engine model name to its meaning.
checks.hint: Use the manufacturer's own key for IO-520-X, then the features the GTSIO manual lists.
checks.rationale: Continental's manual reads I as fuel injection, O as horizontally opposed cylinders and 520 as the displacement in cubic inches. The G prefix marks the propeller reduction gearing.

checks.question: The GTSIO-520-H develops 375 hp at 2,275 propeller rpm, with a propeller drive ratio of 0.667:1. At about what crankshaft rpm is that?
checks.hint: The propeller turns at 0.667 times the crankshaft speed, so divide the propeller rpm by the ratio.
checks.rationale: 2,275 / 0.667 is about 3,411 rpm. The reduction gear lets the crankshaft turn a third faster than the propeller, where the engine makes more power.

checks.question: Why is a reduction gear fitted between the crankshaft and the propeller of a high-power engine?
checks.hint: Think about the propeller blade tips as they spin faster.
answers: It lets the engine run at higher rpm while the propeller turns at a speed where it stays efficient
It makes the propeller turn faster than the engine
It reduces the number of cylinders needed
It removes the need for a propeller governor
checks.rationale: Higher engine rpm gives more power, but propeller efficiency falls rapidly when the blade tips approach the speed of sound. The reduction gear separates the two speeds.

checks.question: Why is induction icing less of a danger with fuel injection than with a float carburetor?
checks.hint: Where does the temperature drop from fuel vaporisation happen in each?
answers: The temperature drop from vaporisation takes place in or near the cylinder, not in the venturi and throttle
Fuel injection uses warmer fuel
Injected engines have no throttle
Fuel injection does not vaporise fuel
checks.rationale: A float carburetor discharges fuel in the venturi, so the cooling happens there and ice can form. An injection system delivers fuel near the cylinder.

checks.question: Put the air-cooled heat-transfer path in order.
checks.hint: Begin inside the cylinder structure and end in the atmosphere.
checks.rationale: Fins increase surface area so heat in the cylinder metal can transfer to cooling air and then to the atmosphere.

checks.question: Why are baffles important in an air-cooled engine installation?
checks.hint: Cooling air must pass across the surfaces that need it.
answers: They direct cooling air across the cylinders and fins
They ignite the fuel-air mixture
They drive the coolant pump
checks.rationale: Baffles control the airflow path so air does useful cooling work instead of bypassing the finned surfaces.

checks.question: An engine burns 4 gallons of aviation gasoline a minute. One gallon holds enough heat to boil 75 gallons of water, and about one-quarter of the heat becomes power. How many gallons of water could the heat that must be removed each minute boil?
checks.hint: First find the heat in all the fuel burned in a minute, then take away the quarter that becomes power.
checks.rationale: 4 x 75 = 300 gallons for all the fuel. A quarter becomes power, so three-quarters, 225 gallons' worth, must be dissipated every minute.

checks.question: What happens to the air-fuel mixture in a cylinder that is too hot?
checks.hint: Think about when the charge is supposed to start burning.
answers: It is preheated and burns before the planned moment, causing detonation and knocking
It stops burning altogether
It burns more slowly and more cleanly
It turns to liquid
checks.rationale: An overheated cylinder preheats the mixture so combustion starts too early. The handbook names premature combustion, with detonation and knocking, as one of three reasons excessive heat is undesirable. The others are weaker parts and poor lubrication.

checks.question: In flight, a pilot closes the cowl flaps. What tends to happen to the engine temperature?
checks.hint: The flaps change the exit area at the rear of the cowling. What does a smaller exit do to the airflow?
answers: It tends to rise, because less air flows over the cylinders
It tends to fall, because the air is trapped
It does not change
It falls because the flaps add drag
checks.rationale: Closing the flaps shrinks the exit area, so less air flows over the fins and carries away less heat. Opening them does the opposite, at the price of extra drag.

checks.question: Put the liquid-cooled heat path in order.
checks.hint: Begin inside the cylinder structure and end in the atmosphere.
checks.rationale: Heat passes from the metal into the coolant, the pump carries the coolant to the radiator, and the radiator gives the heat to the air. A liquid system adds the coolant and radiator steps to the air-cooled path.

checks.question: Match each cooling part to its job.
checks.hint: Some parts belong to air cooling and some to liquid cooling. What does each one do to the heat or the flow?

pairs.right: Increase the surface that touches the cooling air
Direct the air close around each cylinder
Change the exit area to control the airflow
Passes heat from the coolant to the air
Give the warm coolant room to expand

checks.rationale: Fins add surface, baffles steer the air, and cowl flaps meter it. In a liquid system the radiator passes heat to the air and the expansion tank with its pressure cap lets the coolant expand safely.

checks.question: Why is pure water not used as an engine coolant, even though it carries heat so well?
checks.hint: Think of a cold night and of a very hot cylinder head.
answers: It freezes, boils and promotes corrosion
It carries too little heat
It is too expensive
It is flammable
checks.rationale: Water is cheap and carries heat well, but it freezes and expands, it boils and forms steam pockets, and it promotes corrosion. Glycol and additives answer those faults, at the cost of some heat capacity.

checks.question: What is the trade-off of a waterless coolant compared with a conventional glycol and water mix?
checks.hint: It will not boil. What does it give up?
answers: A high boiling point, but a lower heat capacity and so slightly higher running temperatures
A lower boiling point and better heat capacity
It is cheaper but corrodes the engine
It needs no pump
checks.rationale: Rotax says a waterless coolant prevents boiling because of its high boiling point, but its lower specific thermal capacity gives slightly higher running temperatures.

checks.question: Match each engine to its cooling method.
checks.hint: Think of each engine by name: a trainer engine, a wartime V-12, a light-sport engine with two kinds of cooling, a 1927 Atlantic flier.
checks.rationale: The GTSIO-520 is air cooled, the Merlin is a liquid-cooled V-12, the Rotax 914 combines liquid cooling of its heads with ram air on the cylinders, and the Whirlwind that flew the Spirit of St. Louis is an air-cooled radial.

checks.question: A flying club wants an engine for a trainer that is light, simple and cheap to maintain. Which cooling method suits best, and why?
checks.hint: Which method has fewer parts to carry and look after?
answers: Air cooling: no coolant, pump or radiator to carry or maintain
Liquid cooling: it always gives more power
Liquid cooling: it never needs maintenance
Neither: trainers do not need cooling
checks.rationale: Air cooling needs only fins, cowling and baffles, so it is lighter and simpler with less maintenance. Liquid cooling is chosen when the extra power or temperature control is worth its weight and complexity.

checks.question: How many crankshaft revolutions does a two-stroke engine need to complete one operating cycle?
checks.hint: Compare it with the 720 degrees of a four-stroke cycle.
answers: One
Two
Four
checks.rationale: A two-stroke engine needs one upstroke and one downstroke, so it completes the cycle in one revolution.

checks.question: In a two-stroke cycle, which functions are accomplished during the same stroke?
checks.hint: Think about the ports that open near the bottom of the stroke.
answers: Intake and exhaust
Compression and ignition
Power and compression
checks.rationale: The intake and exhaust functions are accomplished during the same stroke, which is how one revolution is enough.

checks.question: What is at the heart of a rotary (Wankel) engine?
checks.hint: There are no reciprocating pistons.
answers: A three-sided rotor turning inside an elliptical housing
A double-acting piston in a long cylinder
A rotating cylinder block around a fixed crankshaft
checks.rationale: The rotary cycle uses a three-sided rotor in an elliptical housing; the events occur in the chambers between rotor and housing.

checks.question: Which statement best describes the crankcase?
checks.hint: Think about what has to stay aligned and what the cylinders bolt to.
answers: The rigid foundation that holds the crankshaft bearings, supports the cylinders and provides mounting for the powerplant
The chamber in which fuel and air are burned
The part that meters fuel to each cylinder
checks.rationale: The crankcase contains the bearings and supports in which the crankshaft revolves, supports the cylinder assemblies and the mounting lugs, and must stay rigid to prevent misalignment.

checks.question: What are the three main parts of a crankshaft?
checks.hint: Two cheeks and one of these make a throw.
answers: Journal, crankpin and crank cheek
Piston, ring and pin
Main bearing, cap and bolt
checks.rationale: Every crankshaft has journals that turn in the main bearings, crankpins to which the rods attach, and crank cheeks joining them.

checks.question: Which connecting-rod type is used in inline and opposed engines?
checks.hint: It has a cap and a two-piece bearing at the crankpin end.
answers: Plain
Master-and-articulated
Fork-and-blade
checks.rationale: Plain-type rods suit inline and opposed engines; master-and-articulated rods are used in radials and fork-and-blade rods mainly in V-type engines.

checks.question: What do oil control rings do?
checks.hint: Compression rings deal with gas; these deal with the other fluid.
answers: Scrape surplus oil from the cylinder wall and return it to the crankcase
Seal combustion gas above the piston crown
Hold the piston pin in place
checks.rationale: Compression rings seal the combustion gases; oil control rings limit oil reaching the combustion chamber and return the surplus to the crankcase.

checks.question: How is the aluminium cylinder head joined to the steel barrel?
checks.hint: Temperature is doing the work.
answers: The head is heated and screwed onto the chilled barrel, forming a gastight shrink joint
The two are welded along the cooling fins
They are bolted together with a gasket between them
checks.rationale: The head is expanded by heating and screwed onto the chilled barrel; as they equalise the joint becomes gastight.

checks.question: Which bearing type carries both radial and thrust loads?
checks.hint: Think of the bearing that holds propeller thrust.
answers: Deep-groove ball bearing
Straight roller bearing
Plain bushing
checks.rationale: A deep-groove ball bearing controls both radial and thrust loads; a straight roller bearing carries radial load only.

checks.question: How does the GTSIO-520-H drive its propeller?
checks.hint: The manual describes a quill shaft.
answers: Through a quill shaft and reduction gear to a flanged propeller shaft
Directly from a flange formed on the crankshaft
Through a belt drive
checks.rationale: The crankshaft's internal spline mates with a quill shaft that drives the reduction gear, which drives the flanged propeller shaft; a direct-drive engine such as the IO-520 has the propeller flange on the crankshaft itself.

checks.question: Put these in the order force passes through them during the power stroke.
checks.hint: Start where the expanding gas meets the engine and finish at the shaft that turns.
items: Expanding gas pushes on the piston
The piston pin passes the load to the connecting rod
The connecting rod turns the crankpin
The crankshaft rotates and drives the propeller shaft
checks.rationale: Gas pressure on the piston is carried through the pin and rod to the crankpin, and the crankshaft turns the reciprocating force into rotation that drives the propeller.

checks.question: Which of these is a moving part of the engine?
checks.hint: Moving parts do the work. Stationary parts hold things in place.
answers: The connecting rod
The crankcase
The cylinder barrel
The mounting lug
checks.rationale: The connecting rod moves with the piston and the crankshaft. The crankcase, the cylinders and the mounting lugs are the stationary structure.

checks.question: What force does the crankcase have to resist at each cylinder pad?
checks.hint: Think about what the burning gas pushes on besides the piston.
answers: The force tending to pull the cylinder off the crankcase
A force trying to push the cylinder deeper into the case
The weight of the propeller only
Nothing: the cylinders carry their own loads
checks.rationale: The handbook notes that the tremendous forces on the cylinder tend to pull it off the crankcase, which is why the cylinders are held on studs and the case must be stiff.

checks.question: Match each part to its typical material.
checks.hint: Think about which parts need to be light, which need strength, and which face extreme heat.

pairs.right: Heat-resistant steel such as nichrome or cobalt-chromium
Soft non-ferrous alloy such as bronze or lead-tin

checks.rationale: Each material is a compromise: light and strong aluminium for the case and piston, forged alloy steel for the shaft, heat-resistant steels for the hottest valve, and soft alloys for bearings that must give way before the shaft.

checks.question: Why is the cylinder head of an air-cooled engine made of aluminium alloy?
checks.hint: Two properties of the metal help the cooling and the weight.
answers: It conducts heat well and is light
It is the hardest metal available
It is cheaper than steel and does not corrode
It does not expand when heated
checks.rationale: The handbook gives aluminium alloy for air-cooled heads because it is a good conductor of heat and its light weight reduces the overall engine weight. Deep fins can be cast in it.

checks.question: On the ground, which engine-mount bolts carry the weight of the engine?
checks.hint: Think about which bolts hold the engine up, and which stress is added in flight.
answers: The upper bolts; in flight a torsional stress is added to all of them
The lower bolts only
All bolts equally, and no extra stress in flight
The bolts hold nothing; the rubber carries the weight
checks.rationale: The upper bolts support the weight of the engine on the ground. In flight a torsional stress is added to all the bolts, which is why only the special heat-treated steel bolts may be used.

checks.question: What do rubber-and-steel shock mounts do?
checks.hint: They sit between the engine and the airframe.
answers: Let the engine move a little so that vibration is damped before it reaches the airframe, with snubbers limiting extreme movement
Fix the engine rigidly to the airframe
Cool the engine mount
Carry the engine's fuel to the carburetor
checks.rationale: The rubber deforms slightly and damps vibration, and metal snubbers limit the movement under abnormal shocks or loads.

checks.question: Tap the crankcase.
checks.hint: It is the foundation: the cylinders bolt to it and the mounting lugs are on it.
checks.rationale: The crankcase holds the crankshaft bearings, supports the cylinders and carries the mounting lugs. On this model the crankcase and its mounts are one part.

checks.question: Tap the propeller reduction drive.
checks.hint: It sits at the front of a geared engine, between the crankshaft and the propeller.
checks.rationale: The GTSIO-520-H is geared: a reduction gear at the nose drives the propeller shaft at 0.667 times crankshaft speed. A direct-drive engine has no such gear.

checks.question: Tap the piston pin.
checks.hint: It passes through the piston and the small end of the connecting rod.
checks.rationale: The full-floating pin joins the piston to the connecting rod and turns freely in both. Soft aluminium plugs at its ends keep it from scoring the cylinder wall.

checks.question: Tap the cylinder barrel.
checks.hint: It is the steel part below the finned head, where the piston slides.
checks.rationale: The barrel is steel, nitrided inside to resist wear. The aluminium alloy head with its deep fins is shrunk onto it.
